nodes.source: A Promising Physical Method for Recovery of Licoo 2 and Graphite from Spent Lithium-Ion Batteries Grinding Flotation

description: grinding flotation is a source-specific Process entity in the study A Promising Physical Method for Recovery of Licoo 2 and Graphite from Spent Lithium-Ion Batteries Grinding Flotation. Scope: Grinding flotation experiments were carried out in standard Hardgrove apparatus and lab-scale flotation machine. First, 40 g of mixed electrode powder together with steel balls were sealed in the grinding chamber. The grinding times were 2.5 min, 5 min, 10 min, 20 min and 30 min, respectively. Then, the grinding productions were subjected to reverse flotation with the same experimental conditions. Quantitative observations concern: LiCoO2, graphite.

process.overview: Electrochemical recovery (ER) of base metals using a trough flow-cell with a 304 stainless steel mesh cathode (6 cm x 30 cm, 40 mesh, submerged area ~28 cm x 6 cm) and a carbon felt anode with Pt wire current collector, distance 3.5 cm. Leaching solution (0.1 M Fe2(SO4)3 in 1 M H2SO4 or 0.2 M FeCl3 in 0.5 M HCl) pumped through a packed bed column (15 cm Tygon tubing, 1 inch ID, 70 g grinded non-ferrous cell phone material) at 3 mL min^-1. Total 310 mL leaching solution loaded; after filling cell, recirculation started and current density 138.9 A m^-2 applied using galvanostat/potentiostat. Samples taken every 30 min initially, then hourly for Fe3+ measurement. Stopped when Fe3+ conversion through column <10%. Deposit and undissolved e-waste weighed and digested for analysis.

process.overview: After the three-phase plate electromagnetic separation, the belt type 1-disc separator was applied to the material with grain sizes below 1 mm. The raw material was loaded through a hopper onto a conveyor belt that transported it into the slit under a rotating disc. Magnetic particles were caught by the rotating disc and thrown outside the magnetic field, while non-magnetic material was directed below the plate surface and transferred to a container. Separation was performed with a 2 A electric current through the windings and a working gap of 2 mm. This yielded two magnetic and one non-magnetic fraction.

process.overview: Ten used mobile phones were mechanically disassembled, batteries separated, and the remaining material cut with a guillotine. Samples were introduced in a heat-resistant mesh basket into a laboratory bubbling fluidized bed reactor at 800–850 °C for three minutes to decompose organic components; the solid residue was then pulled out. The reactor was a 10 kW unit with a transparent quartz cylindrical tube (100 mm outer diameter, 500 mm height, 2–3 mm wall thickness) on a perforated chrome-nickel steel distributor plate (1 mm thickness, 0.6 mm holes, 1.8% open area). Air and propane–butane gas were fed through the distributor. Initial bed conditions before sample introduction were 840–860 °C at 50 mm above the distributor, 6.5% O2, 10% CO2, and 20 ppm NOx. Exhaust gas composition and bed temperature were monitored.
equipment: laboratory bubbling fluidized bed reactor (10 kW)

process.overview: The fraction below 1 mm was subjected to two-stage separation. Initially, a three-phase plate electromagnetic separator was used. This device had a flat plate of transformer metal plates with windings connected to a three-phase power supply, producing three independent oscillating magnetic fields on a near-vertical positioned plate. Tests were performed with an electric current of 80 A in the windings. Material moved vertically by gravity while magnetic fractions also moved horizontally, allowing separation into magnetic and non-magnetic fractions.

process.overview: Fig. 9 shows the alteration of the leaching efficiency of Li as a function of HCl - H2O2 ratio in the range of 1:0–25:1 by using HCl concentration of 3 M, S/L of 1:50, leaching time of 90 min and leaching temperature of 80 ^∘C. It can be observed from Fig. 7 that the leaching efficiency of Li was 97.1% without H2O2. And it reached to 99.4% with HCl - H2O2 ration being 10:1. A conclusion can be drawn from the experiment that H2O2 had a slight role in the leaching process of Li. In the leaching process for Hydrometallurgy, H2O2 was added as reductant to convert undissolved high valence ions to soluble low ones to promote the reaction process. Because of the absence of intermediate valence of Li, H2O2 can reduce Co(III) to Co (II) and thus facilitate the forward reaction. The result shows that the amount of H2O2 was sufficient for the complete dissolution of lithium, as further increasing the concentration of H2O2 did not show a significant effect in the recovery efficiency compared to consumption of expensive of lithium. Considering lower energy consumption and relatively better leaching efficiency, the suitable leaching agent was HCl without H2O2.

process.overview: As described above, the main forms of Li in the anode active material are Li2CO3,, Li O, LiF, ROCO Li, CH OLi. Because some of them are water-soluble, such as ROCO2 Li CH3OLi Li2O,, in the experiment performed it has a high leaching efficiency of lithium (84%) only in deionized water. While others are almost insoluble in water and inlaid in the anode active materials, such as ROCO Li, LiF, and they will occur decomposition reaction in HCl solution. Therefore, the leaching reaction between anode materials and HCl solution is a multiple process (Aurbach et al., 2002; Jiangfeng et al., 2004): (1) the hydrolysis of lithium salt (2) double decomposition reaction between lithium salt and HCl solution.

process.overview: Bioleaching of Co and Li from spent LIB powder using a mixed culture of SOB (Alicyclobacillus sp.) and IOB (Sulfobacillus sp.) acclimated for 30 d with 0.25–1.0% (w/v) LIB powder. Media contained 4.0 g/L mixed energy substrates (sulfur and pyrite), incubated at 30 °C until pH ~1.0 and ORP ~450 mV, then spent LIB powder added to 2% (w/v) final concentration after adjusting pH to 1.0. Varied pulp density (1%, 2%, 4%), energy substrate dose (2.0, 4.0, 8.0 g/L), pH control (pH 2.0 by H2SO4 addition), and temperature (30, 35, 40 °C). Controls: cells-free media, pure H2SO4 at pH 1.0, H2SO4 pH 1.0 + FeSO4 2.0 g/L, H2SO4 pH 1.0 + Fe2(SO4)3 2.0 g/L. All in triplicates.

label: H2SO4 leaching with C6H12O6

process.overview: Leaching of spent LFP battery cathode materials using H2SO4 as leaching agent and C6H12O6 as reducing agent. The leaching solution volume was fixed at 45 mL in a 100 mL beaker, with a volume fraction of C6H12O6 to H2SO4 of 1:9. Experiments were conducted under conventional water bath heating with magnetic stirring or ultrasonic-assisted conditions (40 kHz, 40–100 W, acoustic energy density 0.89–2.22 W/mL). Temperature was maintained at target values. After leaching, solid-liquid separation was done by vacuum filtration and metal concentrations were measured by ICP-OES to calculate leaching rates.

evidenceSpan: Fig. 9 shows the alteration of the leaching efficiency of Li as a function of HCl - H2O2 ratio in the range of 1:0–25:1 by using HCl concentration of 3 M, S/L of 1:50, leaching time of 90 min and leaching temperature of 80 ^∘C. It can be observed from Fig. 7 that the leaching efficiency of Li was 97.1% without H2O2. And it reached to 99.4% with HCl - H2O2 ration being 10:1. A conclusion can be drawn from the experiment that H2O2 had a slight role in the leaching process of Li. In the leaching process for Hydrometallurgy, H2O2 was added as reductant to convert undissolved high valence ions to soluble low ones to promote the reaction process. Because of the absence of intermediate valence of Li, H2O2 can reduce Co(III) to Co (II) and thus facilitate the forward reaction. The result shows that the amount of H2O2 was sufficient for the complete dissolution of lithium, as further increasing the concentration of H2O2 did not show a significant effect in the recovery efficiency compared to consumption of expensive of lithium. Considering lower energy consumption and relatively better leaching efficiency, the suitable leaching agent was HCl without H2O2.

evidenceSpan: As described above, the main forms of Li in the anode active material are Li2CO3,, Li O, LiF, ROCO Li, CH OLi. Because some of them are water-soluble, such as ROCO2 Li CH3OLi Li2O,, in the experiment performed it has a high leaching efficiency of lithium (84%) only in deionized water. While others are almost insoluble in water and inlaid in the anode active materials, such as ROCO Li, LiF, and they will occur decomposition reaction in HCl solution. Therefore, the leaching reaction between anode materials and HCl solution is a multiple process (Aurbach et al., 2002; Jiangfeng et al., 2004): (1) the hydrolysis of lithium salt (2) double decomposition reaction between lithium salt and HCl solution.

evidenceSpan: Highest amounts of all six REEs, i.e., La (361 ppm), Nd (821 ppm), Gd (75 ppm), Pr (100 ppm), Sm (55 ppm) and Ce (20 ppm) were recovered from power supply boards.

sourceEntityEvidence: Fig. 9 shows the alteration of the leaching efficiency of Li as a function of HCl - H2O2 ratio in the range of 1:0–25:1 by using HCl concentration of 3 M, S/L of 1:50, leaching time of 90 min and leaching temperature of 80 ^∘C. It can be observed from Fig. 7 that the leaching efficiency of Li was 97.1% without H2O2. And it reached to 99.4% with HCl - H2O2 ration being 10:1. A conclusion can be drawn from the experiment that H2O2 had a slight role in the leaching process of Li. In the leaching process for Hydrometallurgy, H2O2 was added as reductant to convert undissolved high valence ions to soluble low ones to promote the reaction process. Because of the absence of intermediate valence of Li, H2O2 can reduce Co(III) to Co (II) and thus facilitate the forward reaction. The result shows that the amount of H2O2 was sufficient for the complete dissolution of lithium, as further increasing the concentration of H2O2 did not show a significant effect in the recovery efficiency compared to consumption of expensive of lithium. Considering lower energy consumption and relatively better leaching efficiency, the suitable leaching agent was HCl without H2O2.
